I have uploaded the manuscript to OpenEvidence and received high quality feedback. Overall assessment: not yet submission-ready. As written, this reads as a well-organized software/technical note with a genuinely useful contribution (a transparent, open ANSI S3.5 implementation plus an inspectable gain rationale), but it would likely be rejected or returned for major revision at JASA in its current form. The core problems are (1) a validation section that claims "clinical efficacy and safety" while presenting only self-referential simulations, (2) several internal inconsistencies between text, equations, tables, and reference list, and (3) unsupported priority and precision claims. None of these are fatal to the underlying work — they are fixable — but all would be flagged by a JASA reviewer in Speech Perception/Psychological and Physiological Acoustics.

Most serious scientific problem: circular and overstated validation

Section VI states the goal was "to validate the clinical efficacy and safety" of Open-NL, but the predicted SII values were computed with the author's own sii() engine, and no listener data, real-ear measurements, or loudness judgments were collected. A self-computed index applied to self-derived targets is a consistency check, not validation. Efficacy and safety claims for a prescription require behavioral outcomes; the comparative literature on NAL-NL2 versus DSL v5.0 is built on aided speech recognition, REM, and questionnaire data in real patients. 
[1-4] The word "validate" should be replaced with "benchmark," and clinical/safety language removed throughout, including the abstract.

This matters clinically, not just rhetorically. Open-NL prescribes substantially less gain than DSL v5.0 (and often less than NAL-NL2) at 4–8 kHz in the A4–A7 profiles per Figure 2, and the manuscript frames the lower sone values as an advantage. In a retrospective series of 635 ears, speech recognition was best when REAR met or exceeded DSL v5.0 targets and worst when it fell >5 dB below
<truncated 5917 bytes>
t but should be cited rather than asserted. 
[6-7]

Limitations section. Currently absent. It should state that no human verification was performed, that targets are proxies rather than validated rationales, and that Open-NL is not intended for clinical fitting in its present form. Given the infant RECD and MPO modules, an explicit statement that the software is for research and education, not pediatric clinical fitting, is warranted.

Formatting and style

The bulleted lists in Sections III.B and V are rendered as inline asterisks (lines 87–91, 194–198) rather than true lists — a LaTeX/markdown conversion artifact. Figure captions duplicate "Figure 1: Figure 1:". Equation numbering runs to 21, which is heavy for a technical note; consider moving the module-level equations to an appendix or supplementary document. Article type should be confirmed against current JASA categories, since the text self-describes as a "Technical Note" while the structure resembles a full research article. The LLM acknowledgment is appropriately worded and consistent with current disclosure norms.

Bottom line

The concept is publishable and the transparency argument is legitimate. Before submission, prioritize: verify the SII engine against ANSI reference cases; recheck and correct Table I (the loudness values in particular appear erroneous); fix the Margolis and Studebaker citations; remove all efficacy/safety and validation language; add a limitations section; and reconcile the equation-level inconsistencies. Framed honestly as an open-source computational tool with a transparent, explicitly proxy gain rationale and no behavioral validation, the manuscript would be considerably more competitive than in its current form.

Would you like a point-by-point revision plan for the benchmarking section, including what a defensible non-behavioral verification protocol against ANSI S3.5-1997 reference cases would look like?
</USER_REQUEST>

Overall, this reads as a competent JASA Technical Note in structure and typesetting, but in its current form it would likely draw a major-revision decision on three grounds: unsupported or mis-attributed citations, a "validation" section that contains no validation, and internal inconsistencies between the results table and the narrative claims. The core contribution (open-source ANSI S3.5 engine + transparent prescription proxy) is publishable; the framing around it overclaims.

1. Citation and attribution problems (highest priority)

    The Margolis reference appears mis-cited. The reference list gives "Speech Recognition in Hearing Impaired Listeners: 1. A Cochlear Distortion Metric," JASA 157(4), 2932–2941. The paper that develops the Normal/Low/Moderate/High distortion classification from predicted-vs-measured word recognition (n = 9928 ears) is titled "Predicted and measured word-recognition scores unmask distortion in the impaired auditory system," JASA, April 2025. Verify the exact title, volume, and pages before submission — JASA copyediting will catch this. [1]

    The transfer function is attributed to the wrong word list. Line 192 states the "Studebaker et al. (1993) NU-6 transfer function," but the cited Studebaker, Sherbecoe, and Matesich (1993) paper is on CID W-22 lists (per the reference list itself). NU-6 and W-22 have different frequency-importance and transfer functions; this is a substantive, not cosmetic, error given Eq. 20 drives the entire distortion module. Also note the author is "Sherbecoe," not "Sherbec."

    Section III.H (75% ABG) cites nothing. "Adhering to standard clinical practice" is exactly the sentence a reviewer will flag. Cite Johnson (2013), which is the source that formalizes the 75% ABG + BC convention, demonstrates that "75% ABG + BC" and "25% ABG + AC" are not interchangeable in a nonlinear prescription, and documents NAL's use of it since NAL-NL1. Two further points belong there: (a) the rationale is that the compression ratio should track the sen
<truncated 5124 bytes>
el" (line 163), and "first algorithm to computationally integrate" (lines 11–12, 189 — priority claims are hard to defend and add nothing). Also, DSL v5.0's own handling of the conductive component is a separate adjustment layer rather than a 75% rule, so avoid implying the three algorithms treat mixed loss equivalently in the benchmark.

5. Smaller items

    Bullet lists at lines 87–91, 194–198, and 213–222 render as literal asterisks in the compiled PDF. Convert to a proper itemize environment.

    Figure captions duplicate "Figure 1: Figure 1:".

    The anonymized dashboard URL (euphonic-euphemism.github.io) and the data-availability repo (github.com/mshaver/SII) are inconsistent; reconcile before submission.

    Eq. 3 has a "−3" embedded and then a parenthetical stating a global 3 dB reduction is "subsequently applied" — as written the reduction is applied twice or once, unclear. Clarify.

    "SII" is used as both the index and the package name; italicize or use a distinct package name to avoid collision.

    CR_loud in Eq. 18 can go below 1.0 (expansion) for large HTL_sn at low frequencies; add an explicit floor of 1.0 or state that expansion is intended.

    The Acknowledgments LLM disclosure is appropriate and well worded.

Suggested single highest-yield revision: reposition the paper as a transparent, reproducible computational framework whose prescription module is explicitly a research proxy requiring empirical validation, and add a short "Limitations and future directions" section naming the absence of human REM verification, the A6 audibility deficit, and the untested status of the distortion-driven roll-offs. That framing is defensible with the data actually presented.

Would you like a drafted replacement for Section III.H that states the 75% ABG convention with its correct provenance, rationale, and the explicit caveat that the fraction is not preference-validated?

Yes — this is a clear net improvement, but it is not yet at an acceptance threshold. The revision fixes most of the citation errors, adds a Limitations section and an ANSI verification claim, and correctly downgrades the overclaiming language. However, it introduces new problems, weakens the paper's central novelty by deleting the Margolis distortion section, and still leaves the two most consequential prior objections only partially addressed.

What genuinely improved

    Johnson and Dillon (2011) is now correctly cited — the actual title is "A Comparison of Gain for Adults from Generic Hearing Aid Prescriptive Methods: Impacts on Predicted Loudness, Frequency Bandwidth, and Speech Intelligibility." That paper does exactly what is needed here: seven hypothetical hearing losses, 1/3-octave insertion gain from each method's own software, diffuse-field-to-eardrum transform, Moore–Glasberg loudness, and ANSI S3.5-1997 SII. [1]

    The 75% ABG convention is now properly attributed to Johnson (2013), with an honest caveat that the exact proportion is empirically unsettled.

    The MHL and CIN modules are now anchored to the NAL-NL3 fitting system (Kitterick et al.), which is legitimate and timely. NAL-NL3 launched with exactly a Prescription plus a Comfort in Noise Module and a Minimal Hearing Loss Module, and the CIN Module is described as a comfort-focused profile for noisy environments that reduces listening fatigue while maintaining intelligibility. [2-3]

    The abstract now correctly distinguishes published derivations from closed reference implementations, which is the accurate and defensible version of the "black box" argument.

    Overclaiming largely removed: "validate the clinical efficacy and safety" → "benchmark the computational behavior"; "mathematically guarantees a perfectly smooth" → "provides a continuous"; the Moore–Glasberg claim replaced by an honest "proxy model" description.

    Eqs. 4 and 6 now have the missing outer max(0, ·), correcting a real bug that would
<truncated 3491 bytes>
iograms N1–N7 (plus S1–S3 for steeply sloping); calling them "A1–A7" and describing all as "sloping high-frequency" profiles remains inaccurate. The Bisgaard set is widely used and machine-classifiable as a canonical taxonomy, so nonstandard labels will be flagged. [4]

    ANSI verification is asserted, not shown. Section V.E is three sentences with no numbers. Add a table of computed vs. standard reference SII values with residuals; this is the single highest-yield addition and would take one page.

<USER_REQUEST>
Lead with the package name and what it computes; drop "prescriptive algorithm" and "mathematically transparent" entirely. Software-paper titles are indexed and cited by tool name, and the guidance for software papers is that the title should make the software's identity and function immediately findable rather than advance a scientific claim. [1] The current title makes two claims a software venue will not evaluate (that Open-NL is prescriptive, and that transparency is a result), and buries the package name.

A structural problem to settle first

The package is named SII and the algorithm is named Open-NL. A title cannot foreground both without implying the prescription is the contribution. Decide which artifact the paper is about:

    If the paper is about the ANSI engine plus dashboard, the title should say SII and the Open-NL generator becomes a described feature.

    If the paper is about Open-NL, the venue should not be JOSS-as-a-methods-paper, and the earlier concerns apply.

For the split strategy previously discussed, the first option is correct.

JOSS titles

JOSS convention is a short name-first phrase, typically no verb and no claim:

    SII: An R package for Speech Intelligibility Index calculation and hearing-aid gain target generation

    SII: Speech Intelligibility Index computation and WDRC target generation in R

    SII: An open-source R implementation of ANSI S3.5-1997 with an interactive WebAssembly dashboard

The first is the safest. It names the standard-based core function first and the target generator second, which matches the actual strength ordering of the work — the ANSI engine is verified against Annex B and C, the gain generator is not validated.

R Journal titles

The R Journal favors slightly more descriptive titles that state the package's scope:

    SII: Speech Intelligibility Index calculation and configurable hearing-aid gain shaping in R

    Computing the Speech Intelligibility Index in R: the SII package and an interactive shinylive interface

Words to remove, and why
Current wording	Problem	Replacement
"prescriptive algorithm"	Asserts clinical prescription status the paper cannot support; invites clinical review at a software venue	"gain target generation" or "gain shaping"
"mathematically transparent"	A property of open source, not a finding; reads as marketing	omit (open-source implies it)
"dynamic compression"	Vague; WDRC is the indexed term	"WDRC" or omit
"Open-NL" in the title	Elevates the least-validated component to the headline	move to abstract and body
No package name	Software papers are cited by tool name	lead with "SII:"

[1]

One naming caution beyond the title

SII as a package name is a generic acronym, and the paper describes it as a resurrection of an archived CRAN package under the original namespace. If the intent is to keep that namespace, state it plainly in the paper and in the DESCRIPTION, and confirm the handover with the original maintainer is documented — JOSS reviewers check repository provenance, and the manuscript's acknowledgment of transferred maintainership should be mirrored in the repository itself, not only in the paper.

Also note the internal inconsistency the title change must not paper over: the repository URL given is github.com/r-gregmisc/SII while the dashboard is hosted at euphonic-euphemism.github.io/Open-NL/. A JOSS submission requires a single canonical repository, and two different organizational namespaces for one project will be flagged at pre-review.

<USER_REQUEST>
Adding a Loudness Model Would Materially Strengthen the Paper

Adding Moore & Glasberg loudness (sones) alongside SII is the right move, and it directly addresses the circularity objection — but only if it is framed as a two-dimensional trade-off analysis, not as validation. SII alone cannot evaluate Open-NL because Open-NL is tuned to maximize SII. Loudness is an independent, non-tuned axis, so a target that achieves comparable SII to NAL-NL2/DSL at comparable or lower predicted loudness is a genuine, non-tautological finding. This is precisely the design Johnson and Dillon used, and it is the established template in this literature. [1-2]

The precedent to follow

Johnson and Dillon compared NAL-NL1, NAL-NL2, DSL m[i/o], and CAMEQ2-HF across seven hypothetical hearing-loss configurations (five sensorineural, one mixed, one conductive), computing 1/3-octave insertion gain, applying a diffuse-field-to-eardrum transfer function, then feeding eardrum output levels into both the Moore & Glasberg loudness model and ANSI S3.5-1997. [1]

Their benchmark numbers are the ones to reproduce and cite as the calibration anchor:
Anchor value	Result	Why it matters for Open-NL
NAL-NL2 and DSL m[i/o] overall loudness, 65 dB SPL ILTASS, 5 SNHL configs	~8 sones	The target corridor Open-NL should land in [1]
Normal-hearing listener, same input	18.6 sones	Confirms validated prescriptions deliberately undershoot normal loudness — Open-NL's global −3 dB reduction can be defended against this [1]
NAL-NL1 and CAMEQ2-HF	Greater loudness	Illustrates the upper end of acceptable variation [1]
Predicted SII across methods at conversational levels	Differences "largely negligible"	Critical caveat: SII will not discriminate between prescriptions at 65 dB SPL [1]

That last row is the most important consequence for the manuscript. Ching et al., analyzing 200 children, reached the same conclusion — prescription choice had minimal effect on predicted speech intelligibility but marked effects on predicted loudness. [2] This m
<truncated 2408 bytes>
nnot be regenerated natively — an honest constraint the paper should state rather than work around.

    Outputs per configuration, per input level (50/65/80 dB SPL ILTASS): 1/3-octave insertion gain, ANSI SII, and overall loudness in sones via Moore & Glasberg, with specific loudness patterns for at least the reverse-slope and steep-slope cases. [1]

    Presentation: A gain-deviation panel plus an SII-vs-sones scatter with each prescription as a point per configuration. That single figure carries the whole argument.

    Bandwidth/excitation: Johnson and Dillon also reported bandwidth of cochlear excitation, which is worth including given Open-NL's high-frequency desensitization and dead-region modules. [1]

Two caveats on implementation

    The Moore & Glasberg model version matters. CAMEQ2-HF was built on an improved loudness model for impaired hearing distinct from earlier versions, and the binaural summation extension is separate again. Specify exactly which iteration is implemented and whether monaural or binaural, since binaural summation shifts sone values substantially (level difference for equal loudness ~5.6 dB at 500 Hz, 4.2 dB at higher frequencies in impaired listeners). [5-6]

    Reimplementing the loudness model in R is a nontrivial, separately verifiable component. It needs its own verification table against published Moore & Glasberg outputs, exactly as done for the ANSI Annex B/C check. Otherwise the paper has added a second unverified engine rather than an independent yardstick.

Net effect on venue fit

This addition moves the manuscript from "unvalidated heuristic" to "characterized heuristic," which is the standard a software paper can realistically meet. It makes the R Journal / JSS route substantially stronger and would make an audiology-journal submission defensible. For JOSS it is still surplus to requirements — that version should cut the analysis to the repository.

As for as sone levels for DSL5, they are still too high. Yes — 36 sones would be far outside anything a DSL v5 fitting predicts for a mild-to-moderate loss at conversational input. In the Johnson and Dillon modeling, DSL m[i/o] and NAL-NL2 both produced approximately 8 sones overall loudness for a 65 dB SPL speech input across five sensorineural configurations, versus 18.6 sones for a normal-hearing listener with the same input. [1] A value of 36 sones is roughly 4–5× the prescribed loudness and nearly double normal-hearing loudness — i.e., beyond what an unaided normal ear experiences for conversational speech.

Context for interpreting a 36-sone figure:

    DSL is the "louder" of the two rules, but not by that margin. Its higher prescribed gain relative to NAL produces meaningfully greater predicted loudness across input levels while SII differences remain small, but the difference is on the order of a few sones, not a 4-fold multiple. Note that loudness in sones is a doubling scale — each doubling of sones equals a perceived doubling of loudness — so 8 → 36 is more than two perceptual doublings. [2-3]

    Likely explanations for such a number, in order of probability:

        The input level is not 65 dB SPL. A high-level input (80 dB SPL, or an MPO/loud-speech curve) will yield much higher modeled loudness, and DSL prescribes higher output than NAL-NL2 at both 65 and 80 dB SPL. [4]

        The loss is not actually mild-to-moderate, or the fitting is substantially over target. Deviation from DSL targets grows with degree of loss and with steeply sloping configurations. [5]

        The units are categorical loudness (CU, 0–50 scale) rather than sones — these are numerically similar in magnitude for a "loud" rating but are not interchangeable with sones.

        The value is a per-ear-summed or binaural figure rather than a monaural overall loudness.

    Clinical implication if the value is genuinely monaural loudness at conversational input: the fitting is almost certainly over-amplified, and loudness discomfort, rejection, and non-use are the expected consequences. Preferred listening level in compression fittings sits within about 5 dB of MCL, with mid-level speech placed at MCL and only high inputs slightly above. Verification should return to real-ear dB SPL against DSL v5 targets (±5 dB, or ≤5 dB RMSE at 0.5/1/2/4 kHz), and MPO should be checked against measured or threshold-predicted LDL, since the acceptable SSPL window is wide for mild losses but the risk is over-shooting comfort rather than under-shooting audibility. That study found trained real-world preferred gain was reached from a start-up point 6 dB below NAL-NL1, with better loudness satisfaction — it supports a conservative offset, not its removal. As written, the sentence uses Mueller to justify the opposite of what the data showed. Removing the −3 dB offset is defensible on the Johnson & Dillon loudness argument alone; drop the Mueller attribution or reframe it as a countervailing finding. [5-6]

    The Leijon anchor is stated imprecisely (§III.B). Leijon's 40–50% figure applies specifically to cases with incomplete loudness recruitment; with complete recruitment and widened filters the model gives 25–30% for mild-to-moderate loss and a nonlinear increase with severity. Since µ = 0.40–0.50 is applied uniformly across all degrees of loss, the current text over-claims derivation. State the recruitment assumption explicitly. [7]

    The one-third rule is applied to the wrong quantity (§III.C). Byrne & Murray, and Byrne & Dillon, describe variation in audiogram slope requiring about one-third as much variation in response slope, relative to a baseline response — not a one-third-of-differential low-frequency penalty pinned at 250 Hz. Equation 3 borrows the coefficient without the baseline, so the citation does not support the formula as written. Two further problems compound this:

    Leijon's modeling found prescribed responses needed a less steep bass cut than NAL, which cuts against any additional LF suppression in this configuration. [7]

    The steep-slope branch (Eqs. 6–9) still uses the unchanged 20 dB penalty with a 30 dB knee. Two adjacent slope-correction rules now use incompatible derivations — a reviewer will notice immediately.

    Speed and ratio are still conflated (§III.G), and Hornsby & Ricketts is inverted. Windle et al. is a compression speed trial; its 35 dB HL boundary predicts preference for slow-acting compression, not for a lower ratio. Hornsby & Ricketts found that consonant-recognition decrements from higher compression ratio were largest at 65 dB SPL and essentially absent at 95 dB SPL — the opposite of the manuscript's claim that aggressive compression "applied to high-level inputs" degrades the envelope. If the goal is to defend CR ≤2:1, Neuman et al. is the direct citation: paired-comparison quality preference fell with increasing CR, with ratios ≤2:1 significantly preferred over >3:1, and linear preferred in the highest-level noise. Overall assessment

The manuscript is internally coherent and unusually candid about its own limits, but the central problem is a mismatch between title/framing and content: the title promises a "theoretical rationale," while the text itself states Open-NL is "a multi-stage parameterized shape generator, not a derived rationale." Almost every module is labeled by the authors as an "unvalidated exploratory design assumption," and the evaluation shows the cascade produces bidirectional loudness dispersion, including severe under-amplification (1.3 and 2.8 sones for A4/A5) in exactly the population where real-ear data show speech recognition is most vulnerable. [1] A rationale, in the NAL sense, is a derivation from an explicit optimization objective plus empirical correction; a stack of hand-set constants is not. [2-3] The honest reframing is "a transparent, modifiable computational implementation" rather than "a theoretical rationale."

The core theoretical gap

NAL-NL1/NL2 were obtained by optimizing a speech-intelligibility model subject to a loudness constraint, then adjusted by empirical preference data (sex, experience, degree of loss, bilateral fitting, compression preference in severe loss). [3] DSL and CAMEQ2-HF likewise derive from stated objectives (audibility/desired sensation level; loudness equalization). [4] Open-NL has no objective function. Section II acknowledges the circularity of using SII to evaluate an SII-tuned heuristic — but the paper never states what Open-NL is actually optimizing. If the answer is "nothing; it is a parameterized shape generator," that belongs in the abstract and title, not buried in Section I.

A second structural issue: the paper argues the cascade order exists "to prevent unintended interactions," then Section I.F concedes that the severe-loss booster and the high-frequency desensitization envelope are competing mechanisms that mathematically undo each other in profound high-frequency loss. Overall assessment

The manuscript is unusually candid — the repeated "unvalidated exploratory heuristic" labeling and the explicit non-clinical disclaimer are appropriate and should be retained. The core problem for the sections of interest is a mismatch between the strength of the cited evidence and the specificity of the constants derived from it: most of the numerical rules (−10 dB reverse-slope floor, 20 dB LF penalty, 60 dB booster knee, 45 dB Lgain, 12 dB LDL buffer, +5 dB salvage, 1.5:1 CIN clamp) are not traceable to the cited sources, and several citations are either misattributed, incomplete, or contradicted by a stronger paper the manuscript does not cite. There is also a load-bearing internal inconsistency about whether Open-NL optimizes anything.

The central theoretical inconsistency

Section I states Open-NL "lacks a formal optimization objective," yet Section II's circularity argument rests on Open-NL's gain shaping being "tuned specifically to maximize the mathematical ANSI SII metric." Both cannot be true, and the second claim is what motivates the entire loudness-versus-SII evaluation design. As written, the framework is a cascade of shape heuristics, so the circularity concern is largely unearned — and the results (Open-NL achieving the lowest SII in the dataset for A4 and A5) actively refute it. Reframing Section II as "no tautological advantage exists because there is no optimization step" would be more defensible and would strengthen, not weaken, the paper.

Relatedly, the NAL philosophy is explicitly loudness normalization — maximize speech understanding subject to loudness at or below normal — while Open-NL has no loudness constraint in its cascade at all. [1] The MPO/LDL ceiling is an output-safety cap, not a loudness-normalization constraint. This should be stated plainly as the fundamental architectural difference from NAL-NL2, and it is the direct mechanistic explanation for the bidirectional dispersion reported in Table I.

This is a substantial improvement and most of the prior structural problems are genuinely fixed: the LaTeX corruption is gone, µ has been removed cleanly, Leijon's incomplete-recruitment range (40–50%) is now correctly matched to the implemented 0.46, the reverse-slope rule has explicit equations, the ablation table is restored, the Methods Note explains the comparator recomputation, the A2 deficit is disclosed, the A5 superiority claim is appropriately downgraded to comparability, and the appendix cross-reference is corrected. Three problems remain that a reviewer will catch, one of which is a functional bug.

Equation 6 is dead code

Equation 3 defines Slope = max(0, PTAHF − PTALF), which by construction is never negative. Equation 6 then computes RSfactor = (−Slope − 15)/20, which for any non-negative Slope is ≤ −0.75 and clamps to zero. The reverse-slope branch can never activate. The manuscript needs a signed slope variable (or a separate reverse-slope differential) for Equations 6–7 to function.

There is a second, more consequential issue in Equation 7. In the original manuscript the −10 dB flattening was applied to Cinterp, the correction array. Equation 7 now applies it to Gbase, the total gain — meaning a fully-triggered reverse-slope case is prescribed −10 dB of total insertion gain across the low frequencies. That is not gain suppression; it is attenuation below unaided. Given that reverse-slope losses often have genuinely poor low-frequency thresholds, this would be clinically indefensible if the branch ever fired. Restore the correction-array formulation and state the trigger threshold explicitly.

Overall assessment

The manuscript is honest, unusually well-caveated, and technically legible, but its central rationale is under-argued. It is best framed as a software/tools paper, not a prescriptive-method paper. The core problem: the stated motivation — transparency as an alternative to "opaque runtime optimizers" — conflates implementation opacity with derivational opacity, and the paper never establishes that this is a real gap. NAL-NL1/NL2 rationales are published in detail (maximize SII subject to loudness ≤ normal, with named empirical adjustments), and the loudness and SII models used in their derivation are open in the literature. [1-3] What is proprietary is the compiled software, not the rationale. Substituting a cascade of hand-set constants for a stated optimization objective trades one form of unaccountability (closed code) for another (unjustified magic numbers), and the manuscript should say so directly.

The central rationale problem: a heuristic without an objective function

Section I concedes that Open-NL "lacks a formal optimization objective," yet the abstract and conclusion claim it "empirically lands near the NAL-NL2 loudness range" and "mirrors the clinical safety and stability of NAL-NL2." These are in tension. If there is no objective, near-agreement with NAL-NL2 on some audiograms is a coincidence of parameter choice, and disagreement (A2, SII 0.52 vs 0.81) is equally arbitrary. Recommended reframing: Open-NL is a parameterized shape generator with an exposed API whose value is pedagogic and exploratory, not a prescriptive rationale. The paper's own sentence to that effect should be moved to the abstract.

    The 0.46 anchor. The justification chain (Lybarger half-gain → Byrne & Dillon → Leijon's incomplete-recruitment 40–50%) is a post-hoc rationalization of a single scalar. The manuscript's central premise — that the derivations of NAL-NL2 and DSL m[i/o] are public but their implementations are closed, and that this blocks component-level ablation — is a defensible and honestly framed motivation. Weaknesses and Concerns in the Theoretical Rationale

    The half-gain anchor is theoretically regressive. NAL-NL2 derives its gain through formal constrained optimization maximizing SII subject to a loudness ceiling. Open-NL instead starts from a 0.46 × HTL half-gain rule (Lybarger, 1944) and then patches it with cascaded heuristic modules. The manuscript acknowledges this but understates the conceptual gap: NAL-NL2's slope-dependent behavior emerges from its optimization, whereas Open-NL must manually engineer it via the SD-LFP. This means Open-NL's behavior in untested audiometric configurations is unpredictable — it lacks the theoretical generalizability of an optimization-derived formula. The 2D sensitivity surfaces partially address this but cannot substitute for formal optimization across the full audiometric space. [1-2]

    The uncapped severe-loss booster relying on "downstream parameter collisions" is architecturally fragile. The manuscript argues that safety is guaranteed by collision between the booster and L_gain/SD-LFP modules. However, this emergent safety property depends on the specific parameter values chosen for all interacting modules simultaneously. If a researcher modifies one module (which is the stated purpose of the tool), the collision may no longer hold. The sensitivity surface (Figure 2) shows insensitivity across the tested parameter space, but the tested ranges are narrow relative to what a researcher might explore.

Why 10.0 sones is defensible but suboptimal

A fixed 10.0-sone ceiling is roughly 25% above the NAL-NL2 average of ~8 sones, which provides reasonable headroom. However, the problem is that NAL-NL2 does not use a fixed sone ceiling — it uses a degree-of-loss-dependent loudness constraint. The empirical data from the manuscript's own Table I illustrates why this matters:

    Mild/moderate profiles (A1–A3): NAL-NL2 produces 5.8–8.1 sones. A 10.0-sone ceiling here is too generous — the optimizer will exploit the surplus loudness budget by over-amplifying, producing targets louder than NAL-NL2 intends.

    Severe/profound profiles (A4–A5): NAL-NL2 produces 11.1–11.9 sones — already above the 10.0-sone ceiling. A fixed 10.0-sone cap here artificially constrains the optimizer, potentially explaining the A4 result (SII = 0.44 vs NAL-NL2's 0.53) — the optimizer may be sacrificing intelligibility to comply with a ceiling that NAL-NL2 itself exceeds.

A more defensible approach

Rather than a single fixed value, consider a degree-of-loss-scaled ceiling anchored to the Johnson & Dillon data:

    Option 1: Scale to the NAL-NL2 empirical envelope. Use the NAL-NL2 predicted loudness for each profile's PTA as the ceiling (e.g., ~6 sones for mild, ~8 for moderate, ~12 for severe). This directly mirrors the NAL philosophy and can be justified by citing the official NAL-NL2 outputs from the same software generating the comparison targets.

    Option 2: Use 18.6 sones (normal-hearing loudness) as the absolute ceiling with a soft penalty ramp starting at ~8 sones. This aligns with the NAL-NL2/NL3 philosophy of keeping loudness at or below normal levels, while allowing the optimizer to trade loudness for intelligibility in severe losses where NAL-NL2 itself exceeds 10 sones. [2]

    Option 3: If a single fixed value is preferred, the most defensible choice would be approximately 12 sones — the upper bound of NAL-NL2's own range across sensorineural profiles (A4 = 11.9 sones in the manuscript's Table I). This avoids artificially constraining severe losses while still preventing catastrophic recruitment. However, this would still over-budget mild losses.

Recommendation

Option 1 or 2 would be strongest for publication. A PTA-scaled ceiling directly maps to the NAL philosophy and is justified by the Johnson & Dillon (2011) empirical data. [1] It would also likely resolve the A4 deficit — if the ceiling is raised to ~12 sones for that profile, the optimizer gains the freedom to find a higher-SII solution. This scaling could be implemented as a simple linear function of PTA (e.g., ceiling = 6 + 0.1 × PTA, clamped at 18.6), which would be transparent and easily modifiable by researchers.

<USER_REQUEST>
Reframe the thesis away from "SII superiority" toward "transparent computational substrate"

The single most important editorial fix. As currently written, the abstract and results present higher predicted SII at matched loudness as evidence of superiority over NAL-NL2, but the field's own literature undercuts this. Johnson and Dillon—the very source of the A1–A7 benchmark profiles—showed that across generic methods, insertion-gain differences produce "by and large negligible" differences in predicted speech intelligibility at conversational levels, and that high-frequency audibility becomes progressively less effective for intelligibility as loss worsens. [1] A tool that claims SII gains of 0.03–0.26 over NAL-NL2 is therefore making a claim the modeling literature says is unlikely to be perceptually meaningful. Recast the contribution as what it actually is—an open, inspectable, modifiable optimization testbed—and demote the head-to-head SII tables to illustrations of how objective/constraint choices redistribute spectrum, not evidence of a better formula. This reframing also resolves the reviewer's likely objection that the loudness cap is reverse-engineered from NAL-NL2, making the comparison partly circular.
1.
A Comparison of Gain for Adults From Generic Hearing Aid Prescriptive Methods: Impacts on Predicted Loudness, Frequency Bandwidth, and Speech Intelligibility.
Journal of the American Academy of Audiology. 2011. Johnson EE, Dillon H.

Confront the SII's known limitations head-on rather than in an appendix

A JASA reviewer will immediately flag that the objective function is an audibility index that poorly predicts individual performance. This should be addressed in the main text, not deferred to the distortion appendix. Bernstein et al. showed in JAAA that individualized auditory-processing models incorporating spectrotemporal modulation sensitivity predict speech recognition significantly better than the audibility-based SII. [2] Hülsmeier and Kollmeier quantify the non-compensable Plomp distortion component and show the clinical audiogram alone yields substantially higher SRT prediction error than models incorporating suprathreshold measures. [3] Citing this work to explicitly bound the interpretability of an SII-maximizing objective would preempt the most predictable criticism and demonstrate scholarly command of the domain.

Strengthen the loudness-model treatment and address binaural summation

The loudness constraint is monaural, but recent JASA-adjacent work shows binaural broadband loudness summation in hearing-impaired listeners is on average ~13 dB higher than normal and exceeds the normal range in ~40% of patients—with direct implications for gain targets. The new validation section is the biggest liability

The two experiments in Section IV are the right experiments to run, but the reported results are so perfect that they will read as a red flag rather than reassurance—and they partly contradict the manuscript's own text.

    The convergence result is not credible as written and is internally contradictory. Reporting that across 140 runs the optimizer "converged to the exact same theoretical global optimum" with an SII standard deviation of "exactly 0.00000" for every profile directly contradicts the paper's repeated (and correct) statements that Nelder-Mead is "vulnerable to local minima or premature termination on highly irregular objective surfaces (such as the steep slopes of the A4 and A5 profiles)" and that constraint enforcement is "heavily dependent on the heuristic seed configuration." Both claims cannot be true. Either the objective surface is smooth enough that seeds do not matter (in which case the entire SD-LFP "necessity" ablation and the local-minimum narrative collapse), or the surface is irregular and ±2 dB perturbation with 20 restarts is far too gentle a test to demonstrate global convergence. A reviewer will read zero variance as evidence that the perturbation was cosmetic. Fixes: (1) perturb far more aggressively (e.g., ±15–20 dB, or draw seeds uniformly across the plausible gain space, not just near the tuned seed); (2) report the full distribution of final SII and the number of distinct optima found, not just the SD; (3) benchmark against an independent global optimizer (differential evolution, simulated annealing, or multi-start L-BFGS-B) and show agreement; (4) reconcile the result with the local-minimum narrative—if the A7 optimizer "conservatively arrests at a local minimum," then a global-convergence claim for A7 is contradictory and must be resolved.

    "0.00 sones maximum violation" over 100 audiograms proves less than claimed. A soft penalty on the objective does not structurally guarantee constraint satisfaction, as the text itself concedes. Finding zero violations in 100 draws may simply reflect that the penalty weight is high enough that the optimum never lands near the boundary for these draws—it does not bound worst-case behavior. Strengthen this by: reporting how close the finalized loudness comes to the cap (the distribution of slack), deliberately constructing adversarial audiograms designed to stress the uncapped severe-loss booster and large ABGs against the ceiling, and increasing n well beyond 100 (100 is trivial to compute and undersells an open testbed whose whole advantage is cheap large-scale simulation). Also specify how the 100 audiograms were generated (threshold distributions, inter-frequency correlation, ABG prevalence) so the space is reproducible and defensibly "plausible."

    Report the machinery. Convergence tolerance, max iterations, penalty weight, simplex reflection/expansion parameters, and random seed are all needed for reproducibility and are currently absent.

Missing \value-tags in .Rd-files
Problem

Every .Rd file should have an \value-tag stating what the output of the function is. Even if nothing is returned, the \value-tag is necessary for CRAN.
Solution

Often it is enough to simply add the missing \value-tags. If the function doesn’t return anything, write that as your \value-tag.
Details
CRAN Review Communication

CRAN wants a \value-tag for every .Rd-file containing info about the structure of the output (class) and also what the output means.

Adding a short explanation for each function helps users understand effects of the function call. This prevents unexpected outputs and helps to create a better workflow when using the function.

The only exception are .Rd-files for data sets, marked with the \docType{data}-tag. Since these are no functions, no \value-tag is necessary.

Sometimes functions don’t return one specific value but are rather called for their side effects. In that case the \value-tag should state this.

\value{No return value, called for side effects}

When using ‘roxygen2’ to render the .Rd-files, an @return-tag must be added in the corresponding .R-file. This will create the \value-tag automatically when rendering.

#' @return What your function returns.

For more details on ‘roxygen2’ check the ‘roxygen2’ section.
Repeated Rejections of Issues in Manuals If Using ‘roxygen2’
Problem

The CRAN team rejected your package for issues regarding the manuals a second time, even if you already changed them according to their suggestions.
Solution

Implement your changes in the corresponding .R-files instead of the .Rd-files. Before resubmitting render the .Rd-files again using roxygenize().
Details
CRAN Review Communication

If you decide to render your manuals with ‘roxygen2’, the .Rd-files can be rendered using the function roxygenize(). If changes are implemented directly in the .Rd-file, they will be overwritten during the next render. Similarly, changes in the ‘roxygen2’-section of .R-files will not transfer to the .Rd-files without a re-rendering.
Tip

To avoid this mistake, make sure to always call roxygenize() before submitting your package.

If you want to know more on how to use ‘roxygen2’ to create your manuals, take a look at their website.
Note

When using ‘devtools’, the function devtools::document() acts as a wrapper for roxygenize() and can be used to render the .Rd-files.
Overall Checktime
Problem

Automatic CRAN tests give a NOTE saying the overall checktime of your package is too long.
Solution

Reduce the length and quantity of your examples, vignettes and tests.
Details
CRAN NOTE

Check: Overall checktime, Result: NOTE
  Overall checktime 20 min > 10 min

Unwrapped examples, vignettes and tests of packages are run frequently on CRAN’s test servers. The overall time it takes to run all of them should therefore be less than 10 minutes in total.

Write vignettes and tests with fewer iterations, run them on small toy data or provide precomputed results. Focus on writing sensible test and documentation, retaining high code coverage instead of disabling test or removing examples.

General Issues

The General Issues chapter offers practical tips on CRAN submission best practices, essential file and example structuring, and key meta package requirements.
Description Length

The description field in the DESCRIPTION file should be a short paragraph (2+ sentences) on the package’s purpose, motivation and may include further references to the package documentation website. You can also consider the Description length to be similar to a blurb or synopsis written on the inside jacket of a book - brief but informative. A good example of this description length is included in the ‘ranger’ package.
CRAN Review Communication
Structuring of Examples

As part of their documentation most functions have example code in their .Rd-files marked by the \examples{} tag. Examples serve two major purposes for packages on CRAN.

    Show users how to implement the function correctly and what to expect as outcome.
    Allow the CRAN team to perform regular testing of the code.

For several reasons, some examples cannot be run as tests. Therefore, CRAN has several wrappers to structure them. The following list gives a short overview of the most common ones and when to use them.

    Unwrapped:
        Short examples to show the functionality of the code
        CRAN recommends the use of toy examples on small data sets
        Ideally, also cover some edge cases
    \donttest{}:
        Lengthy examples, with execution times longer than 5 seconds
        Examples that download data
        They are tested infrequently on CRAN as well and are also executed when calling example()
    \dontrun{}:
        Unexecutable examples due to missing information (e.g., API calls where a password is needed)
        Examples which require additional software
        Never executed, are automatically marked with a comment (“# Not run:”) in the Help file.
    if(interactive()){}:
        Functions which only run interactively and cannot be used in scripts
        Most commonly, examples for Shiny Apps and

ge but won’t halt the execution
    if(requireNamespace(“packagename”)){}
        Used for examples which need particular packages to run
        Those packages should be listed in the Suggests field of the DESCRIPTION file
    \dontshow{}:
        Treated similarly to unwrapped examples but are not shown to the user
        Great for setting and resetting options or code purely for tests

Important

All wrappers must still be placed inside the \examples{} tag.

Package Size

Ideally, CRAN packages should be under 5 Mb. There are very few exceptions mostly for a larger inst/ folder (and these will trigger flags for every future submission). They must be approved by a CRAN team member and since every accepted version is saved on CRAN, they are very hesitant.

It’s best to minimize the package size. Large datasets can be hosted externally, such as on GitHub, and downloaded when necessary. Consider placing them in a separate data package that requires less frequent updates.

At a upper limit of the package tarball the CRAN policy states 10 Mb. It is recommended to include third-party source software within the package. If that requires larger tarballs, a modestly increased limit can be requested at submission.
Tip

If your package exceeds the recommended 5 Mb limit, it will generate a NOTE in the R CMD check. You can explain why the size is okay by providing details in the cran-comments.md file.
CRAN Review Communication
Communicating with CRAN

For a smooth review process and to provide CRAN volunteers with helpful context on any issues, it’s recommended to CC cran-submissions@r-project.org in your email communications. See the rules and recommendations on the CRAN Repository Policy. This way, any available team member can respond. Additionally, include any updates or explanations related to your package in the submission comments file (cran-comments.md).

Major concern 1: the evaluation is circular, and some conclusions overstate what the data show

The author explicitly acknowledges the tautology—Open-NL is tuned to maximize ANSI SII, so benchmarking its SII against NAL-NL2 with the same sii() engine confers an automatic advantage. This is the correct insight, and it undermines several of the manuscript's strongest-sounding claims. Two specific problems:

    The "breaking the intelligibility–loudness trade-off barrier" claim (A5) is not supported by the reported numbers. Table I shows A5 Open-NL at SII 0.68 / 9.1 sones vs NAL-NL2 0.60 / 9.2 sones. A 0.1-sone loudness difference is within the ≤1.6-sone approximation error the author reports for the loudness engine itself, so the loudness values are effectively indistinguishable. The SII advantage is, by the author's own argument, partly tautological. "Profound efficiency breakthrough" and "breaking the theoretical trade-off barrier" should be softened to a modeling observation.

    The A7 conductive result argues against the efficiency narrative, not for it. Open-NL reaches SII 0.94 but at 10.4 sones versus NAL-NL2's 0.61 at 4.6 sones. That is more than double the loudness for the intelligibility gain—the opposite of the "comparable or lower loudness" efficiency criterion the author defines in Section III. Describing this as "vastly outperforming" conflates raw audibility maximization with efficiency. Similarly, A2 Open-NL produces higher loudness than NAL-NL2 (3.9 vs 2.0 sones), again inconsistent with the framing. The honest summary is that Open-NL trades loudness for SII in a direction that varies by profile, not that it dominates NAL-NL2.

Critically, the field's most relevant comparative data show that prescription choice has minimal effect on predicted speech intelligibility but marked effects on predicted loudness. [1-2] Johnson and Dillon, using the same Moore & Glasberg loudness model and ANSI SII model this manuscript relies on, found NAL-NL2 and DSL m[i/o] gave comparable predicted intelligibility (~8 sones for sensorineural losses at 65 dB SPL) and that added high-frequency audibility became progressively less effective as loss increased. [2] Open-NL's SII-maximization framing sits uneasily with this literature and with Ching et al.'s "effective audibility" work showing that more audibility is not always better because SII overpredicts the usefulness of amplified high-frequency regions in impaired ears. [1][3] The manuscript should engage directly with effective-audibility/desensitization corrections rather than maximizing raw physical-audibility SII.

Major concern 2: the loudness engine is the primary dependent variable but is itself unvalidated

Since the author correctly argues loudness is the only non-circular outcome available, the entire evaluation rests on the calculate_loudness() function—a "numerically optimized hybrid" of Chen et al. (2011) excitation patterns and the Moore & Glasberg (2004) specific-loudness formula. This hybrid is not itself validated against measured loudness or against the reference implementations. The reported approximation error (≤0.012 SII, ≤1.6 sones vs a 1 Hz grid) quantifies internal numerical consistency, not agreement with perceptual loudness or with the canonical Moore & Glasberg output. Given that individual loudness perception is known to require parameters beyond cochlear gain loss and linear attenuation (e.g., a "post-gain"/central-gain term and individualized binaural summation), the manuscript should (a) validate the hybrid against the published Moore & Glasberg model on standard inputs and (b) temper language such as "the clinical accuracy of the Moore & Glasberg model," which claims validity the paper has not demonstrated. Major concern 3: several heuristic anchors are asserted and some conflict with the prescriptive-gain evidence

    Severe-loss booster and the 60 dB HL breakpoint. The manuscript boosts gain above 60 dB HL (Eq. 1 and Eq. 8) and cites the premise that severe-to-profound losses need more than half-gain. The primary source for the half-gain rule breaking down places that transition at roughly 70 dB HL, not 60, and found preferred gain about 10 dB above NAL prescription primarily when 2 kHz thresholds exceeded ~95 dB, with more low-frequency (not high-frequency) emphasis needed in a substantial subset. More importantly, Mueller's evidence-based review found no studies supporting gain greater than the NAL-R/NAL-RP prescription, and three of eleven supported less. A booster that adds gain on top of a half-gain anchor should be justified against this evidence or explicitly flagged as a hypothesis-generating knob rather than an empirically supported rule. The choice of 60 dB HL and slope 0.15 needs a citation or should be labeled as arbitrary alongside the other explicitly-asserted heuristics. [7-8]

    The 0.46 anchor. The justification chain (Lybarger half-gain; Berger et al. showing gain slightly under half in mild losses; Leijon showing flat/loudness-normalizing responses preferred) is reasonable directionally, but Berger and Leijon actually argue that obtained/preferred gain is frequently well below 0.5×HTL—Leijon's loudness-density model yields only 25–30% of threshold for mild-to-moderate loss. Presenting 0.46 as a "deliberate midpoint of a contested range" is defensible only if the paper acknowledges that a large body of that range sits below 0.46, not symmetrically around it. [9-10]

    Reverse-slope −10 dB floor. The author is commendably explicit that this is an asserted heuristic with only single-case/small-sample directional support (Halpin; Van Tasell & Turner). This candor is good; keep it. Halpin et al. specifically support the mechanism (audiometric thresholds can overstate usable apical function). [11]

    75% ABG restoration. Correctly flagged as an unresolved empirical question. Given that the A7 result depends heavily on this rule and drives the loudness cost noted above, a sensitivity analysis across ABG-restoration fractions would strengthen the paper more than the current single-point claim of structural necessity.

The SII framework structurally cannot support the audibility claims for severe/steep losses, and this undercuts the central "recruitment prevention" thesis. The paper's headline mechanism (SD-LFP preventing A5 recruitment) is evaluated with a loudness model, which is reasonable, but the broader claim that Open-NL "identifies wasted energy" and "under-prescription" depends on treating SII as ground truth. Standard SII omits the suprathreshold distortion component, and the gap between predicted and measured word recognition widens systematically with increasing hearing loss and with steeply sloping configurations — exactly the profiles (A3–A5) where Open-NL claims its largest SII advantages. The author cites Margolis et al. 2025 and builds an exploratory distortion module, but the main-text A3–A5 conclusions should be hedged accordingly: a higher raw SII in a severely impaired ear may reflect over-prediction of audibility benefit rather than real gain. The 60 dB HL severe-loss breakpoint conflicts with the cited evidence. Byrne et al. (1990) place the half-gain breakdown nearer 70 dB HL, with preferred gain exceeding NAL only when 2 kHz thresholds approach 95 dB HL, and Mueller's (2005) review found no support for gain structurally above NAL-R/RP. The A2 case is the clearest problem: the optimizer selected a target on a surface that underestimated true loudness by 3.30 sones, then that target is presented as a boundary "finding." The manuscript acknowledges this convergence bias candidly, but the acknowledgment does not fully neutralize it—several Table III/IV conclusions still rest on targets chosen by a biased optimizer. Recommend either (a) re-optimizing directly against the canonical bramslow2004 engine for at least the boundary profiles, or (b) reframing all optimized targets explicitly as "heuristic neighborhood" outputs rather than trade-off findings.

With seven simulated audiograms, one author, no human subjects, and targets generated by maximizing the same metric used to score them, the Pareto-superiority observations (e.g., A5: higher SII at lower sones) are self-consistency artifacts of the optimizer, not findings.
